title: How to avoid freshers' flu at university, and spot the warning signs of meningitis

content.text: 'Freshers' flu' is a common name for a collection of cold viruses that typically spread rapidly when students arrive at university. It's unpleasant but rarely serious, though sometimes it may be genuine flu. Flu is more than just a bad cold and can be particularly serious for people with long-term health conditions, even when those conditions are well managed.
If you’re starting a new term, here's some advice to help you protect yourself on campus and keep ‘freshers' flu’ at bay.
Practise good hygiene
Coughs and sneezes are the main way that colds, flu and COVID-19 spread. To reduce the risk of spreading illness:

If you feel unwell, particularly if you have a temperature, a continuous cough or sneezing fits, you should avoid close contact with other people until you feel better. If you have vomiting or diarrhoea, you should stay away from lectures and social activities, and avoid preparing food for other people, until you have been free from these symptoms for at least 48 hours.
How can I look after myself if I have freshers' flu or a cold?

Make sure you get plenty of rest and sleep, stay warm, and drink plenty of water to avoid dehydration. Medicines such as ibuprofen or paracetamol can help lower your temperature and ease aches and pains.
How can I tell the difference between freshers' flu and meningitis?

The early signs of meningitis can look like a cold or ‘freshers' flu’ and some symptoms may also be mistaken for a hangover. But anyone with meningitis is likely to become much more unwell, very quickly. It's important to familiarise yourself with the symptoms of meningitis, let someone know if you feel unwell and keep checking on anyone who seems unwell.
Common meningitis symptoms may occur in any order and can include:

The bacteria that cause meningitis can also cause sepsis (sometimes called septicaemia), and the two conditions can occur separately or together. It's important to act quickly if you think you or someone else could have meningitis or sepsis.

Call 999 immediately or go to your nearest A&E if you think you or someone else could have meningitis, septicaemia or sepsis. Trust your instincts, and don't wait for all the symptoms, or for a rash, to develop.
Find out more about the signs and symptoms of meningitis on the NHS website, or visit Meningitis Now and Meningitis Research Foundation for further information and support.
Why do so many people get ill when they start university?
With lots of people newly coming together and mixing closely, universities and other higher education institutions can be hotspots for diseases that spread from person to person.
What vaccinations should I consider having?
You should check that you've had:

If you’re moving away from home, register with a GP near your university as soon as possible. Your university may have its own health centre, and you can still access GP care when you’re back home during the holidays.
Check if you're eligible for the 2026 MenB vaccine offer
There is also a time-limited MenB vaccine offer for some young people in 2026. This is separate from the MenACWY vaccine and protects against meningococcal group B bacteria.

You may be eligible if you're starting university for the first time this autumn, or starting at an eligible further education college as a residential student. If you're eligible, you need 2 doses, at least 4 weeks apart. If this may apply to you, find out more about the MenB vaccine programme, and take up the offer of 2 doses.
